title: Paranormal author will tell why 'Everything You Think You Know About The Loch Ness Monster is Wrong' during Nessie tourist attraction talk
excerpt: A renowned UK paranormal author is set to offer an intriguing alternative take on the centuries-old mystery of the Loch Ness Monster.
content:
A renowned UK paranormal author is set to offer an intriguing alternative take on the centuries-old mystery of the Loch Ness Monster.

In a special free talk in Drumnadrochit village tomorrow, France-based Welshman Geoff Holder will offer up his own unique perspective on the legend of the beast purportedly first encountered by Saint Columba in 565 AD.

The ‘critical, but amusing’ presentation is entitled 'Everything You Think You Know About The Loch Ness Monster is Wrong'.

For a self-confessed lifelong lover of fantasy, horror and science-fiction, there is a surprising streak of scepticism running through Geoff’s critique, with particular focus on the media-fuelled 1930s explosion in Nessie stories, sightings and fakery.

But those with an enthusiasm for the paranormal should not be dismayed by this latest offering from the author of numerous books including Zombies from History: A Hunter’s Guide, The Jacobites and the Supernatural, What is a Poltergeist? Understanding Poltergeist Activity, Scottish Bodysnatchers and 101 Things to Do With A Stone Circle .

In a twist towards the end of the talk – an aspect he is keeping under wraps for now – he will deliver a mystical finale, nudging his theories towards the realms of phenomena beyond human and scientific understanding.

“It might sound like I will be a paranormal author speaking sceptically, but only to a point,” Geoff assures us.

“In my conclusion, where I will try to give an indication of what Nessie might actually be, I will be venturing into the paranormal and one potential explanation - and I only say ‘potential’.”

Geoff has also written screenplays aplenty, in the genres of horror, sci-fi, thriller, fantasy, comedy, action and more.

The fascination was kindled as a very young boy growing up in a part of working class Wales where books and literature were not so easily accessible.

“When I was a wee lad, as you say in Scotland, I grew up in a house without any books in a working class area, but we did have a local branch library,” he explained.

“There I discovered books on horror, science fiction and fantasy, but also on monsters. I’ve been fascinated by them ever since I was a child.

“I wrote a book called ‘The Guide to Mysterious Loch Ness and the Inverness Area’ a few years ago in which I covered all the known sightings of Nessie, putting them in their geographical and historical context - when and where they happened - without much of a comment.

“On this tour, what I’m interested in is the context - everything in human life has a context - historical, cultural and often financial.

“So what I’m doing on this tour is taking a critical look at the context and all the elements that have made up Nessie’s contemporary folklore.

“Some of that will be about the natural context, the power of the place, some will be the historical context and a big part will be the role of newspapers actually, which has been absolutely crucial.

“It all starts with the Inverness Courier in 1868 and it is only in 1933 that the story makes it to the Scottish Daily Express in the central belt, then the Scotsman, then the London newspapers.

“By the end of 1934, anyone in Britain anywhere who read a newspaper - local, regional or national - knew about the Loch Ness Monster, so I’ll be looking at the power of newspaper distribution as well.

“I look at what I call the ‘media-verse’. Once the LOch Ness Monster started to sell newspapers, the whole thing snowballs into books, documentaries, that sort of thing.”

Beyond that, Geoff will look at what he calls the ‘tourist-verse’ and ‘money-verse’, among seven different angles he views as important in the Loch Ness Monster story, drawing what he describes as “some critical, but amusing conclusions”.

“I don’t want to give too much away, but I think it is going to be drawing the line between being critical, but highly-entertaining,” he stressed.

“I’m not being a complete sceptic by any means, I’m not dismissing everything, but I’m saying that if you understand the context of all these things that surround Nessie, then it enriches your experience and improves the pleasure and fascination with which we observe the subject.

“In the 1930s, you suddenly have a situation where newspaper editors are putting their reporters on the overnight train to Inverness, saying 'get me copy!’

“Things suddenly pop out of the woodwork, especially when incentives are involved.

“But the hoaxes only worked because people wanted to believe. That’s the whole point.

“Once everyone in Britain knows about the monster, we see more and more of these hoaxes appear.

“But I’m glad to say that the talk will conclude with a venture into the paranormal and that one potential explanation.”

• Geoff’s free talk will be held at the Nessieland visitor attraction in Drumnadrochit at 2pm on Wednesday, October 7, and is followed by a question and answer session open to all.
